account: Toner, Al-Kaisey, Koshy and Lim of the Department of Cardiology, Austin Hospital, Melbourne, reported a case in BMJ Case Reports (published 4 February 2020). The event date is not given. An 80-year-old woman with known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation wore a 24-hour Holter monitor to assess rate control. On returning the monitor she reported feeling her heart “doing a flip” at 19:29. She noted her heart rate had suddenly dropped from 99 bpm to 65 bpm on her Apple Watch Series 3. The Holter showed she had reverted from AF to sinus rhythm at that time. The authors exported 199 watch readings over 22 hours and matched them to the Holter. The watch's average heart rate was 94 bpm in AF and 66 bpm after reversion. No notification, irregular-rhythm alert or electrocardiogram (ECG) app is described: the patient read the heart-rate display herself. The report documents no change in her treatment. The full text was not available from BMJ. The PMC copy is among the sources and names the device.

ai_role.statement: No alert, notification or rhythm classifier was involved. The watch displayed a photoplethysmographic heart-rate estimate, the patient noticed the drop, and the authors compared the readings with the Holter afterwards. The paper does not describe the heart-rate estimation as machine learning. So the AI character of the contribution is not established.

claim_basis: Sources: two independent case reports. The cited evidence includes no finding by a regulator or court.

comparator.quote: A total of 199 heart rate readings were recorded from the Apple Watch and matched to 199 readings of the same time intervals on Holter monitoring over a 22-hour period as shown in figure 2 (median interval 6 min and IQR of 5.75 min). Moreover, the average HR as measured by smart watch in AF prior to reversion was 94 bpm compared with 66 bpm after reversion to SR.

fields.account: Toner, Al-Kaisey, Koshy and Lim of the Department of Cardiology, Austin Hospital, Melbourne, reported a case in BMJ Case Reports (published 4 February 2020). The event date is not given. An 80-year-old woman with known paroxysmal atrial fibrillation wore a 24-hour Holter monitor to assess rate control. On returning the monitor she reported feeling her heart “doing a flip” at 19:29. She noted her heart rate had suddenly dropped from 99 bpm to 65 bpm on her Apple Watch Series 3. The Holter showed she had reverted from AF to sinus rhythm at that time. The authors exported 199 watch readings over 22 hours and matched them to the Holter. The watch's average heart rate was 94 bpm in AF and 66 bpm after reversion. No notification, irregular-rhythm alert or electrocardiogram (ECG) app is described: the patient read the heart-rate display herself. The report documents no change in her treatment. The full text was not available from BMJ. The PMC copy is among the sources and names the device.
